Melt
mĕlt
v. (to dissolve by heat; figuratively, to lose courage; rendering Hebrew masas, mug, Greek luo, teko)
From Anglo-Saxon meltan. Scripture's commonest use is not metallurgical but military: hearts, not metals, are what melt in the Old Testament.

Biblical Definition

Melt in Scripture is chiefly what happens to courage. Moses' song at the sea predicts it — “all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away” (Exo 15:15) — and Rahab reports it fulfilled forty years later in one of the great confessions of the Old Testament: “as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt… for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath” (Jos 2:11). The melting is contagious in both directions: at Ai “the hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Jos 7:5), and Caleb recalls that the unbelieving spies “made the heart of the people melt” while he wholly followed the LORD (Jos 14:8). A report melts a nation, and the report is usually carried by men who were sent to encourage. The word finally turns cosmic in Peter: “the elements shall melt with fervent heat” (2Pe 3:10) — the created order itself proving less solid than it looks.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines melt as to dissolve, to make liquid by heat, and figuratively as to soften to love or tenderness, or to dishearten and deprive of courage.

expand to see more

MELT, v.t. To dissolve; to make liquid; to liquefy; to reduce from a solid to a liquid or flowing state by heat.

2. To dissolve; to reduce to first principles.

3. To soften to love or tenderness.

MELT, v.i. To become liquid; to dissolve. 2. To be softened to love, pity, tenderness or sympathy. 3. To faint; to be discouraged.

Key Scripture

Jos 2:11 — "And as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath."

Exo 15:15 — "Then the dukes of Edom shall be amazed; the mighty men of Moab, trembling shall take hold upon them; all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away."

Jos 14:8 — "Nevertheless my brethren that went up with me made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD my God."

2Pe 3:10 — "But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up."

Modern Corruption

Courage treated as a temperament some possess rather than a fruit of what a man believes about God — while the melting effect of an unbelieving report on a whole congregation goes unreckoned.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglected doctrine is the contagiousness of unbelief. Joshua 14:8 states it without softening: the spies made the heart of the people melt. Ten men with a discouraging report cost a nation forty years. That is a warning to everyone who speaks to God's people — in a pulpit, a small group, or a conversation after the service — because a melted heart is rarely melted by an enemy. It is melted by a brother with a bad report.

The principle to recover is that courage is a function of doctrine, not disposition. Rahab's heart melted at exactly the same news that hardened Jericho's king, and she reasoned from it to a confession — the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath — and then acted. The melting was the beginning of her faith. What a man's fear does to him depends entirely on what he believes about the God who caused it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew masas (H4549), to dissolve, faint, melt away — used of hearts and of manna; mug (H4127), to soften, dissolve; Greek luo (G3089), to loose, dissolve, in 2Pe 3.

expand to see more

Hebrew masas (H4549) — to melt, dissolve, faint; the hearts of Canaan (Jos 2:11) and of Israel at Ai (Jos 7:5).

Hebrew mug (H4127) — to melt, soften; the inhabitants of Canaan melting away in Moses' song (Exo 15:15).

Greek teko (G5080) — to melt with heat; the elements melting at the day of the Lord (2Pe 3:12).

Usage

"“Our hearts did melt… for the LORD your God, he is God” — Rahab reasons from fear to faith."

"“Made the heart of the people melt: but I wholly followed the LORD” — a bad report costs forty years."

"“The elements shall melt with fervent heat” — creation is less solid than it looks."
